case_study_insert.main_stem: Galaxy Lanes and Screens (GLS) is a sole trader in the leisure and entertainment sector, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2008 by Marcus Whitfield, GLS operates an independent cinema and ten-lane bowling venue attracting families and students, and uses a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership, where staff organise their own shifts and events. GLS plans to invest $680,000 in refurbishing the bowling alley and installing two new 4K screens, financed by a $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the projection equipment. It has fixed costs of $1,950,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $18.50, and currently produces 185,000 units a year (one unit is one ticketed visit). GLS faces two problems: casual evening and weekend staff absenteeism stands at 13%, and private-party bookings are being lost to a rival entertainment centre.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2026: GLS sold 16,800 cinema tickets and 9,200 bowling games in Q3; screen occupancy averaged 34% and concession waste is 5.2%. Customer complaints fell from 94 to 61 per month. Market research of 720 visitors found 57% would pay up to $3 more for recliner seating in screen 1, and 48% said the bowling area needs updating; 73 private parties were booked this quarter, up from 41. Review scores average 4.3 out of 5 across 2,150 reviews. Weekend family passes bundle cinema plus one bowling game for $29.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Galaxy Lanes and Screens as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 5.75% to 6.5%, raising borrowing costs on variable-rate expansion loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $10.24 to $10.80 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for casual evening and weekend staff. (3) Commercial electricity and heating prices have risen 13.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on leisure and entertainment grew 3.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: GLS plans to finance part of the refurbishment with hire purchase on the projection equipment. Explain two advantages for GLS of using hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $280,000 projection equipment cost over fixed monthly instalments matched to the screens' earning life, so GLS does not need to commit such a large lump sum from a $400,000 bank loan. This keeps more of the bank loan available for the bowling refurbishment and for absorbing the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices — critical for a venue where the two new 4K screens will run for long evening sessions.

Point 2: GLS gains immediate ownership-style use of the equipment while paying, so the screens can open before full payment is made; interest is built into the instalments, making budgeting predictable; and if cash flow disappoints, the hire purchase provider — not a court — repossesses only the equipment. Unlike a bank loan, no additional collateral over the whole venue is required, preserving GLS's independence as a sole trader under Marcus Whitfield's control and protecting the $5.50 variable cost economics of concession sales that fund the investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Galaxy Lanes and Screens and its refurbishment decision.

questions.question_text: GLS is reopening after its refurbishment with two new 4K screens and an updated bowling alley. Consider local radio advertising, community poster and flyer marketing, or social media marketing. Which should GLS choose to promote the reopening? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Local radio reaches commuters and families across GLS's catchment with frequent, memorable audio spots, and it suits time-sensitive opening offers such as the $29 weekend family pass. It is cheaper than TV and can be repeated heavily, but its audio-only format cannot show the new 4K screens or recliner seating, audience targeting is broad, and younger cinema-goers listen to streaming services rather than local radio.

Community poster and flyer marketing: Posters in schools, colleges, libraries and supermarkets reach exactly the family and student audiences that fill screen 1 and the bowling lanes on weekends. Print is very cheap, locally credible and easy for a sole trader to execute with volunteers; however, reach is small and passive, response is hard to measure, and print cannot compete with video for showcasing the 4K experience or the updated bowling area.

Social media marketing: Organic posts plus paid promotion on social platforms show the recliners, screens and bowling lanes in short video, target families and students within a chosen radius, and let GLS retarget past visitors using the 4.3 out of 5 review audience and the 73 private parties in Q3. Cost is low and results are measurable through ticket sales; the risk is that constant content creation eats staff time under a laissez-faire structure with only 55 employees.

Recommendation: GLS should choose social media marketing. It visually sells the refurbishment that $680,000 bought, reaches both segments (students and families) precisely and measurably, leverages the 4.3 review base and $29 family-pass bundle, and costs far less than radio while outrunning print's passive reach. Radio is rejected as too broad and unable to show the venue; community print is rejected as too passive and unmeasurable, though GLS should pin posters in schools alongside social ads to capture the primary-school birthday-party market where 73 Q3 parties came from.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GLS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GLS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: GLS's casual evening and weekend staff absenteeism stands at 13%. Explain two benefits for GLS of introducing job rotation for its front-of-house casual staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation across the till, concession counter, lanes and clean-up lets casual staff vary tasks every few hours, removing the boredom that drives the 13% absenteeism among young evening workers. Varied work satisfies social and esteem needs (Maslow), keeps energy up during long weekend rushes, and gives GLS the multi-skilled cover it needs when someone calls in sick — preventing half-staffed tills on the busiest nights.

Point 2: Rotated staff understand the whole venue, so they can switch roles instantly when queues form — from popcorn to lane reset — protecting screen occupancy of 34% and pushing the Q3 improvement in complaints (down to 61 a month) even further. Staff gain more skills and experience, which improves retention for a small sole trader that cannot match chain-wage packages, and relieves the reliance on Marcus Whitfield under the flat laissez-faire structure where experienced casuals increasingly self-organise their own shifts and private parties.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GLS's absenteeism, service coverage and refurbishment.

questions.question_text: GLS needs reliable weekend coverage for the reopening. Consider recruiting more full-time permanent staff or training existing casual staff to extend their weekly hours. Which should GLS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Recruiting more full-time permanent staff: Permanent hires would give GLS guaranteed weekend cover, deeper venue knowledge and better continuity for private parties (73 in Q3) and screen-1 recliner pre-sales. They would be on salary though full year, lifting fixed costs of $1,950,000 further and adding commitments after the 5.5% minimum wage rise to $10.80 — expensive if weekday daytimes stay quiet and screen occupancy lingers at 34%. Recruitment also takes weeks, and permanence sits awkwardly with a laissez-faire, flexible operating model.

Training existing casual staff to extend hours: Upskilling current casuals is fast, cheap and directly attacks the 13% absenteeism problem by making loyal staff feel valued; extended hours suit students in term-time and families wanting weekend shifts, and the flat structure lets them self-organise. However, casual staff already miss shifts; adding hours to unreliable workers could backfire, and total additional cost (and the 5.5% wage rise) must be modelled before committing.

Decision: GLS should choose training existing casual staff to extend their weekly hours. It attacks the 13% absenteeism through engagement rather than adding fixed salary cost, fits the laissez-faire flat structure, and can be scaled back if weekday trade stays at 34% screen occupancy. Full-time recruitment is rejected as too rigid and costly ahead of an uncertain post-refurbishment ramp-up; permanent hires only make sense once the 4K screens settle at target occupancy, or for the concession manager role, which should be a permanent hire. GLS should trial extended hours with its three most reliable casuals for one month first, reviewing fit, absenteeism and customer feedback before rolling the scheme across the whole weekend roster.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing options with limited application to GLS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both staffing options in the context of GLS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of GLS with a well-justified decision covering cost, reliability and fit with the flat structure.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GLS's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,950,000 ÷ ($18.50 − $5.50) = $1,950,000 ÷ $13.00 = 150,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 150,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.50 − $5.50 = $13.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $13.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GLS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GLS can compare the 150,000-unit break-even output with actual production of 185,000 visits and games, a margin of safety of 35,000 units, to confirm the venue is comfortably profitable and can support the $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the 4K projection equipment.
2. With $13.00 contribution per unit, management can test promotions such as the $29 weekend family pass (cinema plus one game): bundling lowers per-visit contribution, so managers must model how many extra families the bundle attracts to keep total contribution covering the $1,950,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps GLS decide whether the two new 4K screens lift occupancy above the current 34% enough to clear break-even with room to spare, before Marcus Whitfield commits to further refurbishment phases such as the $3 recliner-seat premium that 57% of visitors said they would accept.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($1,950,000 ÷ 185,000 units + $5.50 = $16.04 a unit) to target the 5.2% concession waste, benchmark weekday versus weekend profitability, and decide whether screen 1 recliner pricing or the $29 family pass better attacks complaints (61 a month) and party-booking losses.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 150,000 units a year, computed as $1,950,000 fixed costs divided by $13.00 contribution per ticketed visit (selling price $18.50 less variable cost $5.50). At the current 185,000 visits, GLS operates a margin of safety of 35,000 units, confirming the venue earns above break-even heading into the refurbishment. (ii) Contribution per unit = $13.00 per ticket or game, the amount every visit adds toward fixed costs and, after that, profit for reinvestment. (iii) Four applied uses: first, checking the margin of safety against the $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase on the 4K projection equipment; second, modelling the $29 weekend family pass, where the halved per-visit contribution must be offset by enough extra family volume to keep total contribution above break-even; third, testing whether two new 4K screens lift the 34% screen occupancy far enough above 150,000 units to justify the investment; fourth, unit-cost benchmarking at $16.04 per visit ($1,950,000 ÷ 185,000 + $5.50) to target the 5.2% concession waste and the 61 complaints a month. Together these uses let Marcus Whitfield test pricing, promotions and refurbishment phases before spending the budget.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GLS's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has GLS's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.20 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.33 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.80 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.00 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $60,000 inventories + $45,000 trade receivables + $75,000 cash = $180,000; 2025 current assets = $55,000 + $60,000 + $105,000 = $220,000. Current liabilities rose from $150,000 to $165,000. 2024: $180,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.20; 2025: $220,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.33. Excluding inventories: 2024 = ($180,000 − $60,000) ÷ $150,000 = $120,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.80; 2025 = ($220,000 − $55,000) ÷ $165,000 = $165,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.00.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved across both measures. Cash rose from $75,000 to $105,000 — sensible ahead of a $680,000 refurbishment — and the stricter measure climbed from 0.80 to exactly 1.00, meaning GLS can now just meet short-term debts without selling concession stock, an important milestone for a sole trader carrying a $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase. Inventories fell to $55,000, showing tighter concession control and lower waste than the 5.2% rate suggests. However, 1.00 is still the bare minimum for the stricter measure, and trade receivables rose from $45,000 to $60,000 — school party bookings and corporate events paying late could easily break that parity again.

Conclusion: GLS's financial position has improved. Both measures rose and the stricter measure reached break-even parity at 1.00, so short solvency is no longer dependent on stock. GLS should hold cash discipline tight, chase party-booking deposits aggressively and avoid drawing more on the hire purchase until the recliner premium (57% would pay $3 more) lifts screen 1 revenue above $1,950,000 fixed costs.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether GLS's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GLS of installing recliner seating in screen 1.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recliner seating responds exactly to the 57% of surveyed visitors willing to pay up to $3 more per ticket, allowing GLS to lift the screen 1 price from $18.50 toward $21.50 ($18.50 + $3.00) and raise contribution per head well above the current $13.00. Recliners also differentiate GLS from the rival entertainment centre that is winning its private-party bookings, supporting premium 'luxury cinema nights', higher food-and-drink spend and better reviews from the 4.3 benchmark.

Disadvantage: Recliner seats are expensive to buy and install, consuming part of the $680,000 refurbishment already stretched by the $400,000 bank loan and $280,000 hire purchase, and they reduce seat capacity per row — screen 1 will sell fewer tickets per showing, so higher ticket prices must fill the gap. If the premium fails with price-sensitive students and families, GLS bears the full cost with higher fixed charges, while complaints (61 a month) could rise if seat mechanisms fail during the first summer of the 4K screens.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GLS's research, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 6.5%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase to $10.80 and the 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will affect GLS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (5.75% to 6.5%): On GLS's $400,000 variable-rate bank loan, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds about $3,000 a year in interest ($400,000 × 0.75% = $3,000), lifting fixed costs above $1,950,000. Higher rates also make consumers more cautious about discretionary entertainment spending, though leisure spending grew 3.1%. The direct impact is the smallest of the three, is fully computable from insert figures, can be neutralised by fixing part of the loan, and unlike input costs does not compound with every hour the venue operates.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $10.80 per hour from April 2026): Appendix 3 gives both rates, so the hourly delta is exactly $0.56 ($10.80 − $10.24 = $0.56). The annual cost cannot be computed because the insert does not state the number of minimum-wage hours; what can be shown is the threshold at which this factor exceeds the interest rise — it does so once GLS pays more than roughly 5,357 minimum-wage hours a year ($3,000 ÷ $0.56 ≈ 5,357), which a 55-employee venue with evening and weekend peaks will comfortably surpass. The rise lands hardest on the casual evening and weekend workforce already at 13% absenteeism, so pay policy, rostering and engagement all matter to contain the true cost.

Electricity and heating prices (up 13.4% year-on-year): Appendix 3 names commercial electricity and heating, the lifeblood of a cinema and ten-lane bowling alley — projectors, 4K screens, pinsetters, lane lighting, fryers and heating for long evening sessions. The insert does not state utilities' share of costs, so any precise total would be invented; even a bound built purely on insert figures favours a heavy impact: applying 13.4% to the entire $5.50 variable cost gives an extreme upper bound of about $0.74 per visit ($5.50 × 13.4% = $0.74), i.e. roughly $136,345 a year if every visit's variable cost were utility — an absolute ceiling, not a forecast. The honest judgement is directional and unavoidable: 13.4% is the steepest percentage rise in Appendix 3, recurs every operating hour, cannot be fixed or refinanced away the way the loan rate can, and cannot be spread over more visits quickly — screen occupancy is only 34%, and Marcus Whitfield's visitors told him they will pay at most $3 more for recliner seating.

Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in electricity and heating prices will have the greatest impact. It is the steepest percentage increase named, recurs continuously across every show and every lane hour, and offers no financing-style fix; it also undermines the refurbished two-4K-screen model precisely when GLS is trying to lift occupancy above the 34% base and justify the $680,000 investment. The 5.5% minimum wage rise to $10.80 is the second serious pressure on the 55-employee casual workforce and interacts with the 13% absenteeism problem, while the 0.75 point interest rise costs exactly $3,000 a year and can be managed by fixing part of the loan — the smallest of the three. GLS should respond with LED and high-efficiency projection, thermostat and lane-lighting schedules, renegotiating its energy contract, lifting screen occupancy via the recliner premium (57% of visitors would pay up to $3 more), and bundling the $29 weekend family pass — attacking energy use directly rather than passing costs to price-sensitive students and families.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GLS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GLS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GLS with a well-justified judgement that energy-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
